course.title: Cybersecurity Fundamentals
course.description: A defensive, first-principles tour of how to keep information and systems safe — from the CIA triad to authentication, encryption, network defense, and incident response. Topic structure adapted from the ACM Computing Curricula security knowledge areas and organized around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0.

questions.prompt: The three classic goals of information security are confidentiality, integrity, and…
questions.explanation: The CIA triad is confidentiality, integrity, and availability — see 'The CIA triad'.

questions.prompt: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from different categories, such as something you know and…
questions.explanation: Factors are something you know, have, or are — see 'Authentication'.

questions.prompt: Which type of encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt?
questions.explanation: Symmetric encryption shares one secret key — see 'Encryption basics'.

questions.prompt: A firewall's primary job is to…
questions.explanation: Firewalls allow or block traffic against a ruleset — see 'Network security'.

questions.prompt: A message that tricks a user into revealing a password is an example of…
questions.explanation: Phishing is social engineering — see 'Malware & social engineering'.

questions.prompt: A cryptographic hash function is designed to be…
questions.explanation: Hashes are one-way and repeatable — see 'Encryption basics'.

questions.prompt: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 function that covers reacting to an active incident is…
questions.explanation: Respond addresses handling a detected incident — see the diagnostic overview.

questions.prompt: The principle of least privilege means users should have…
options: only the access their task requires
questions.explanation: Grant the minimum access needed — a core defensive habit.

lessons.title: The CIA triad and the threat landscape
lessons.grammar_note: CIA here means Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — never the agency.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the three security goals and classify a threat by which goal it attacks. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which letter of the triad does a leaked customer database violate?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Security is usually framed as protecting three properties, the *CIA triad*. *Confidentiality* keeps information visible only to those authorized. *Integrity* keeps information accurate and unaltered. *Availability* keeps systems and data reachable when needed. A *threat* is anything that could harm one of these; a *vulnerability* is a weakness a threat can exploit; *risk* is the combination of how likely and how damaging that would be. Attackers range from opportunistic criminals to insiders and automated bots. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 organizes defense into six functions — Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Ransomware encrypts a hospital's files. It attacks *availability* (staff can't open records) and, if data is stolen first, *confidentiality*. A separate attacker who silently edits a bank balance attacks *integrity*. Same triad, different letter harmed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify which CIA property each harms: (1) a website knocked offline by traffic floods, (2) an email intercepted and read in transit, (3) a tampered software update, (4) a stolen password file. Answers: (1) availability, (2) confidentiality, (3) integrity, (4) confidentiality.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'threat' and 'vulnerability' as the same word — a threat is the danger, a vulnerability is the gap it uses. Mistake: thinking only confidentiality matters. Exit: (a) Which triad property does a defaced-but-online website mainly harm? (b) Risk combines likelihood with what? Answers: integrity; impact.

lessons.title: Authentication, passwords, and MFA
lessons.grammar_note: Authentication (who you are) is not authorization (what you may do).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish the three authentication factors and explain why MFA resists stolen passwords. Warm-up: which factor is a fingerprint?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Authentication* proves identity; *authorization* decides what that identity may access. Authentication uses factors from three categories: something you *know* (a password or PIN), something you *have* (a phone, hardware key, or passkey), and something you *are* (a fingerprint or face). *Multi-factor authentication (MFA)* requires factors from at least two different categories, so a stolen password alone is not enough. Modern *passkeys* replace passwords with a device-held cryptographic key that phishing sites cannot capture. Good password hygiene means long, unique passphrases stored in a password manager — length beats complexity.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: An attacker phishes Ana's password. With MFA on, logging in still demands a code from her phone (something she has), which the attacker lacks — so the stolen password fails. With a passkey, there is no password to phish at all: the login is signed by Ana's device and bound to the real site's domain.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label the factor category — know, have, or are: (1) a six-digit app code, (2) a memorized passphrase, (3) a face scan, (4) a USB security key, (5) a PIN. Answers: (1) have, (2) know, (3) are, (4) have, (5) know.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling a password plus a security question 'MFA' — both are 'something you know', so it is still one factor. Mistake: reusing one password everywhere. Exit: (a) Two codes from the same category count as how many factors? (b) What makes passkeys resist phishing? Answers: one; they are bound to the real site's domain and never leave the device.

lessons.title: Encryption basics: symmetric, asymmetric, hashing
lessons.grammar_note: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is one-way, no key.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell symmetric from asymmetric encryption and explain why hashing is not encryption. Warm-up: which one uses a public and a private key?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Encryption* scrambles readable *plaintext* into *ciphertext* that only a key can reverse. *Symmetric* encryption (for example AES) uses one shared secret key — fast, but both sides must already share the key safely. *Asymmetric* encryption uses a *key pair*: a public key that anyone can use to encrypt to you, and a private key only you hold to decrypt. In practice systems combine them: asymmetric keys exchange a fresh symmetric key, which then does the bulk work — this is how HTTPS protects web traffic. *Hashing* is different: a one-way function (such as SHA-256) turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed, used to verify integrity and to store passwords safely with a *salt*.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Visiting a bank site: your browser and the server use *asymmetric* keys to agree on a shared *symmetric* session key, then encrypt the actual traffic symmetrically because it is faster. Separately, the site stores your password only as a salted *hash* — even if the database leaks, the raw password is not sitting there to read.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Symmetric, asymmetric, or hashing? (1) one shared secret key, (2) a public/private key pair, (3) a one-way fingerprint that cannot be reversed, (4) how a server safely stores passwords, (5) the fast bulk cipher inside an HTTPS session. Answers: (1) symmetric, (2) asymmetric, (3) hashing, (4) hashing, (5) symmetric.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: saying 'the password is encrypted' when a well-built system *hashes* it — encryption can be reversed with a key, a hash cannot. Mistake: thinking a public key is a secret. Exit: (a) Which key may you share freely? (b) Why add a salt before hashing passwords? Answers: the public key; so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables fail.

questions.prompt: A silently altered financial record is primarily an attack on…
questions.explanation: Tampering harms integrity.

questions.prompt: Which pair qualifies as multi-factor authentication?
options: a password and a security question
a password and a phone app code
questions.explanation: Password (know) plus phone code (have) are two categories.

questions.prompt: Symmetric encryption is characterized by…
questions.explanation: One shared key for both directions.

questions.prompt: You may safely publish which of these?
questions.explanation: Public keys are meant to be shared.

questions.prompt: Hashing differs from encryption because it is…
questions.explanation: A hash cannot be reversed to the input.

questions.prompt: A salt is added when hashing passwords in order to…
questions.explanation: Salts defeat precomputed-table attacks.

lessons.title: Network security: firewalls, VPNs, and segmentation
lessons.grammar_note: A firewall filters traffic; a VPN encrypts a tunnel. Different jobs.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a firewall and a VPN each do and why segmentation limits damage. Warm-up: which one hides and protects traffic on untrusted Wi-Fi?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Networks are defended in layers. A *firewall* inspects traffic and allows or blocks it against a ruleset, ideally with a *default-deny* stance (block everything except what is explicitly permitted). A *VPN* (virtual private network) builds an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network, so eavesdroppers on public Wi-Fi see only ciphertext. *Network segmentation* divides a network into zones so that a breach in one area cannot freely reach the rest. The modern direction is *zero trust*: never assume a device is safe just because it is 'inside' the network — verify every request.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: At a cafe, Beto connects to public Wi-Fi and turns on a VPN; the router sees only encrypted tunnel traffic, not his logins. Back at the office, the firewall's default-deny rules block an unexpected inbound connection, and because the finance systems sit in their own segment, a laptop infection in marketing cannot reach them directly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Firewall, VPN, or segmentation? (1) encrypts traffic over public Wi-Fi, (2) blocks traffic that no rule permits, (3) splits a network into isolated zones, (4) enforces default-deny, (5) limits how far an infected host can spread. Answers: (1) VPN, (2) firewall, (3) segmentation, (4) firewall, (5) segmentation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing a VPN makes you anonymous or virus-proof — it protects the traffic in transit, not the device. Mistake: trusting everything 'inside' the perimeter. Exit: (a) What stance blocks all traffic except what is allowed? (b) What does zero trust refuse to assume? Answers: default-deny; that being inside the network means being trustworthy.

lessons.title: Malware and social engineering
lessons.grammar_note: Malware attacks the machine; social engineering attacks the person.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name common malware types and recognize social-engineering tactics. Warm-up: is a phishing email malware or social engineering?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Malware* is malicious software. A *virus* attaches to a file and spreads when it runs; a *worm* spreads by itself across a network; a *trojan* hides inside something that looks useful; *ransomware* encrypts files and demands payment; *spyware* secretly collects data. *Social engineering* attacks the human instead of the code: *phishing* (fraudulent messages at scale), *spear phishing* (a tailored version aimed at one person), and *pretexting* (inventing a believable story to extract information). Defenses combine technical controls (updates, least privilege, backups) with skeptical habits: verify unexpected requests through a second channel.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: An email claims to be IT and says 'your account expires in one hour — confirm your password here'. The urgency and the request for credentials are classic *phishing*. Carla does not click; she opens the company portal directly and, finding nothing, reports the email. No malware ever ran because the human control worked.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each: (1) code that self-replicates across a network with no user action, (2) a fake invoice email urging you to 'verify' a password, (3) software that encrypts your files for ransom, (4) a program disguised as a free game that opens a backdoor, (5) a caller pretending to be your bank to extract a code. Answers: (1) worm, (2) phishing (social engineering), (3) ransomware, (4) trojan, (5) pretexting (social engineering).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming antivirus alone stops phishing — social engineering targets people, so training and verification matter as much as software. Mistake: confusing a self-spreading worm with a file-riding virus. Exit: (a) Which malware type spreads with no user action? (b) What is the best response to an unexpected urgent credential request? Answers: a worm; verify through a separate trusted channel before acting.

items.translation: the three core security goals: confidentiality, integrity, availability
items.example: Ransomware attacks availability, the third leg of the CIA triad.

items.translation: logging in with factors from two or more different categories
items.example: MFA means a stolen password alone cannot unlock the account.

items.translation: encryption using a public/private key pair instead of one shared secret
items.example: HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption to exchange a session key.

items.translation: a one-way function that turns input into a fixed-length fingerprint
items.example: Passwords should be stored as a salted hash, never in plaintext.

items.translation: a control that allows or blocks network traffic against a ruleset
items.example: A default-deny firewall blocks anything not explicitly permitted.

items.translation: fraudulent messages that trick people into revealing secrets or clicking
items.example: The urgent 'confirm your password' email was phishing.

questions.prompt: A default-deny firewall policy means it…
questions.explanation: Deny by default, allow by exception.

questions.prompt: A VPN primarily provides…
options: an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network
questions.explanation: It protects traffic in transit, not the device.

questions.prompt: Which malware spreads across a network without user action?
questions.explanation: Worms self-propagate.

questions.prompt: Spear phishing differs from phishing because it is…
questions.explanation: Targeted rather than mass-sent.

questions.prompt: Network segmentation helps mainly by…
options: limiting how far a breach can spread
questions.explanation: It contains blast radius.

questions.prompt: Zero trust refuses to assume that…
options: being inside the network implies trust
questions.explanation: Verify every request regardless of location.

lessons.title: Applied project: personal security audit and threat model

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Build a written *threat model* and *security audit* for your own digital life. You will not attack anything — this is a purely defensive planning exercise that maps what you protect, what could go wrong, and what you will change.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) List your most valuable assets (accounts, devices, data) and the CIA property each most needs. 2) For your top three accounts, note whether MFA or a passkey is enabled and how the password is stored. 3) Name three realistic threats (for example phishing, a lost phone, a reused password) and one defense for each, mapped to a NIST function — Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, or Recover. 4) Write your incident-response plan in three steps: how you would detect a compromise, contain it, and recover (including where your backups live).

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Every listed asset is tied to a CIA property. ✔ Each top account has a concrete authentication improvement. ✔ Each threat has a specific, defensive countermeasure mapped to a NIST function. ✔ Your response plan covers detect, contain, and recover, and names a real backup location. If all four hold, you have thought like a defender.
